**Bottom line:** Apply the full $60,000 to extra mortgage principal. That $60k, left to compound at the loan's own 6.25% monthly rate for 10 years with no recast, is worth a guaranteed, risk-free, untaxed ≈$111,900 (vs. original $60,000) — because there's no tax shield, this is the real, full hurdle rate. Investing the same $60k in a taxable index fund nets roughly $133,600 after tax if the market delivers its ~9.9%/yr long-run historical average, but only about $68,900–$96,200 under a conservative 2–6%/yr forward-return scenario, and would actually *lose* money in nominal terms if the 2000s "lost decade" (≈‑0.95%/yr) repeated. The breakeven required return is ≈7.8%/yr after tax — below the historical average but above several real 10-year windows, so "equities always beat the mortgage" is favored-but-not-guaranteed here, not a safe default. A formal weighted trade-off (guaranteed return, expected value, downside protection, liquidity, diversification, behavioral value) robustly favors paying down the mortgage; an 80/20 paydown/invest split is offered as a close, more liquidity-preserving alternative for a household that weighs optionality more heavily. Confidence: MEDIUM — the main counterargument is that this leans on a disclosed risk-preference choice (how much weight to put on downside protection) and on historical-return figures that were sourced via web search rather than independently verified at a primary dataset.
